specPoints.text: be able to classify reactions (including those in Unit 1) as addition, elimination, substitution, oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis or polymerisation

primer.text: Organic reactions sort into families by their bookkeeping: addition merges, elimination splits, substitution swaps, redox climbs and falls, hydrolysis lets water wedge, polymerisation chains. This note runs each family through its signature equation so classification becomes instant.

lessons.title: Addition and elimination: molecular bookkeeping
lessons.opening: Two reactants collapsing into one product is the addition signature; one reactant sprouting extra products - typically an alkene plus a small castoff - is elimination. Ethene's conversions give both patterns their textbook examples.
keyPoints: Addition reactions combine two reactants into a single product, classically across the alkene double bond.
Ethene adds hydrogen to give ethane, bromine to give 1,2-dibromoethane, and water to give ethanol.
Elimination reactions produce more products than reactants, usually an alkene plus a small molecule.
Bromoethane with hydroxide under ethanolic conditions eliminates to ethene, water and bromide.

low.restatement: Addition merges everything into one molecule (nothing discarded); elimination throws a small molecule out and leaves a double bond behind.
low.analogy: Addition snaps two LEGO bricks into one assembly; elimination pries one brick off an assembly, leaving a hole (the double bond) behind.
low.examPointer: Count reactant and product species when classifying: 2-to-1 signals addition, 1-to-2+ signals elimination.

medium.restatement: Addition saturates the double bond by spreading two new substituents across it; elimination desaturates by carving a new double bond from adjacent carbons while ejecting a small molecule such as water or a hydrogen halide.
medium.analogy: Addition zips a jacket shut across an open gap; elimination unzips a new gap where none existed.
medium.examPointer: Spot the double bond: formed in elimination, consumed in addition - that is the structural tell for classification questions.

check.stem: Define an addition reaction.
check.modelAnswer: A reaction in which two reactants combine to form a single product, typically across a carbon-carbon double bond.

check.stem: State what elimination reactions typically produce.
check.modelAnswer: An alkene plus a small eliminated molecule such as water or a hydrogen halide.

check.stem: Explain why alkenes are the classic substrates for addition reactions.
check.modelAnswer: The electron-rich double bond opens to accept two new substituents, converting the unsaturated alkene into a saturated single product.

check.stem: Classify: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH and CH3CH2Br -> C2H4 + HBr. State the bond change in each.
check.modelAnswer: First is addition: the C=C is consumed. Second is elimination: a new C=C is created as HBr is ejected.

lessons.title: Substitution and oxidation: swaps and electron loss
lessons.opening: Substitution swaps one atom or group for another; oxidation hands the organic molecule to an oxidising agent, tracked as oxygen gain or hydrogen loss. Bromoethane to ethanol shows the swap; ethanal to ethanoic acid shows the climb.
keyPoints: Substitution swaps an atom or group inside the compound for a different atom or group.
CH3CH2Br + OH- -> C2H5OH + Br- swaps bromide for hydroxide.
Organic oxidation can involve loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen, driven by an oxidising agent such as acidified dichromate, Fehling's or Tollens'.
CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH oxidises the aldehyde to the acid.

low.restatement: A substitution is an exchange at one position on the carbon skeleton; oxidation raises the oxygen content or lowers the hydrogen content of the whole molecule.
low.analogy: Substitution is swapping a house's front door; oxidation is renovating the house by adding a floor (oxygen) or removing bricks (hydrogen).
low.examPointer: The [O] notation stands for the oxidising agent's oxygen equivalent - name a real reagent (acidified dichromate(VI), Fehling's, Tollens') when asked.

medium.restatement: Substitution conserves the carbon skeleton while trading functional groups; oxidation moves the molecule up the oxidation ladder (alkane -> alcohol -> aldehyde -> acid). The oxidising agent is reduced in the same transaction.
medium.analogy: A tenant swap in one room versus a whole-building renovation: substitution trades one fixture, oxidation transforms the building's energy rating.
medium.examPointer: Quote the C2H4Br2-free example equation CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH and name at least one oxidising agent.

check.stem: In CH3CH2Br + OH- -> C2H5OH + Br-, the hydroxide has

options.text: Replaced the bromine atom on the carbon chain
options.explanation: The bromo group is swapped for hydroxyl - the substitution signature.
No oxygen gas forms; hydroxide becomes part of the alcohol.
Bromoethane has no double bond.
Hydroxide is consumed into the product.

check.stem: Organic oxidation can be described as

options.text: Loss of hydrogen or gain of oxygen by the organic molecule
options.explanation: Both descriptions track the oxidation ladder's climb.

options.text: Gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen
options.explanation: Those describe reduction.

options.text: Replacement of one group by another
options.explanation: That is substitution.
That is hydrolysis.

check.stem: CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH shows

options.text: An aldehyde oxidised to a carboxylic acid
options.explanation: Ethanal gains oxygen, climbing to ethanoic acid.

options.text: An acid reduced to an aldehyde
options.explanation: The arrow runs from aldehyde to acid, uphill the oxidation ladder.

options.text: A substitution of hydrogen by oxygen
options.explanation: The transformation is oxidation, not a positional swap.
No water is eliminated here.

check.stem: Which reagent could supply the [O] in the aldehyde oxidation?

options.text: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI), Fehling's solution or Tollens' reagent
options.explanation: All three are standard aldehyde oxidising agents.
That is a reducing agent, supplying [H].
No oxidising power there.
Solvents do not oxidise.

check.stem: The oxidising agent in CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH is itself

options.text: Reduced, as it accepts electrons from the aldehyde
options.explanation: Oxidation and reduction always pair; the agent comes down.

options.text: Oxidised, donating electrons to the aldehyde
options.explanation: The agent receives electrons; it is reduced.
The agent is consumed in stoichiometric redox.
No such product is implied.

check.stem: Define a substitution reaction.
check.modelAnswer: A reaction swapping an atom or group inside a compound for a different atom or group.

check.stem: Name two oxidising agents used for aldehyde oxidation.
check.modelAnswer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) and Tollens' reagent (or Fehling's solution).

check.stem: Explain why the conversion of an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid is oxidation.
check.modelAnswer: The molecule gains oxygen (equivalently loses relative hydrogen content), raising its position on the oxidation ladder while the reagent is reduced.

check.stem: Classify CH3CH2Br + OH- -> C2H4 + H2O + Br- versus the same reagents giving C2H5OH + Br-. What single condition change steers between them?
check.modelAnswer: First is elimination, second substitution; switching from ethanolic to aqueous hydroxide conditions steers the reaction from elimination toward substitution.

lessons.title: Reduction and hydrolysis: hydrogen gain and water splitting
lessons.opening: Reduction is oxidation's mirror: hydrogen gained or oxygen lost, often with lithium aluminium hydride supplying the [H]. Hydrolysis sounds like water doing the splitting - and with chloromethane it does, yielding methanol and hydrogen chloride.
keyPoints: Organic reduction can involve gain of hydrogen or loss of oxygen.
CH3CHO + [H] -> CH3CH2OH reduces the aldehyde to the primary alcohol, the [H] often from lithium aluminium hydride.
Hydrolysis is a reaction with water that splits a compound, e.g. CH3Cl + H2O -> CH3OH + HCl.
The name hydrolysis means splitting (lysis) by water (hydro).

low.restatement: Reduction descends the oxidation ladder - aldehyde back to alcohol - via hydrogen gain or oxygen loss; hydrolysis invites water to cleave a bond and deliver its halves to the fragments.
low.analogy: Reduction is undressing the molecule of oxygen or dressing it in hydrogen; hydrolysis is letting water act as the splitting wedge.
low.examPointer: Keep the [H] agent straight: lithium aluminium hydride reduces; dichromate oxidises - reversing them is a classic error.

medium.restatement: Hydrogen addition saturates or deoxygenates the substrate; water's split into H and OH fragments installs them across the broken bond, as chloromethane shows with methanol and HCl as products.
medium.analogy: Water arrives as a two-handed helper, giving one hand (OH) to the carbon and the other (H) to the departing group.
medium.examPointer: Quote the chloromethane example when defining hydrolysis - it is the note's canonical case.

check.stem: CH3CHO + [H] -> CH3CH2OH is

options.text: Reduction, gaining hydrogen to form the alcohol
options.explanation: Hydrogen gain marks reduction, descending from aldehyde to alcohol.
Hydrogen is gained here, not lost.
No water acts in this equation.
No atom is swapped in place; the whole molecule is reduced.

check.stem: Which reagent typically supplies the [H] for aldehyde reduction?

options.explanation: LiAlH4 is the standard hydride donor for carbonyl reduction.
That oxidises; it cannot supply hydrogen.
Another oxidising agent for aldehydes.
Not a hydride donor in this context.

check.stem: Hydrolysis of CH3Cl gives

options.explanation: Water splits the C-Cl bond, installing OH on carbon and taking Cl as HCl.
No such split occurs.
Neither product appears in hydrolysis.
That is the starting material unchanged.

check.stem: The word hydrolysis literally suggests

options.explanation: Hydro (water) plus lysis (splitting) names the mechanism.
That is hydrogenation, not hydrolysis.
That is reduction's oxygen side.
No combustion is implied.

check.stem: Organic reduction differs from organic oxidation because reduction

options.text: Gains hydrogen or loses oxygen, descending the oxidation ladder
options.explanation: Reduction runs the ladder's downhill direction.
Water is the hydrolysis reagent, not reduction's.
Oxygen gain is oxidation.
Reduction applies across many functional groups.

check.stem: Define a hydrolysis reaction.
check.modelAnswer: A reaction in which water splits a compound, its fragments installing across the broken bond.

check.stem: State the organic products of reducing ethanal with [H].
Explain why aldehyde-to-alcohol conversion is reduction.
check.modelAnswer: The molecule gains hydrogen (equivalently loses relative oxygen content), moving down the oxidation ladder while the hydride donor is oxidised.

check.stem: A student mixes chloromethane with water and detects an acidic product. Identify the products and classify the reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Methanol and hydrogen chloride form; the HCl explains the acidity, and the reaction is hydrolysis - water splitting the halogenoalkane.

lessons.title: Addition polymerisation: monomers into chains
lessons.opening: Addition polymerisation is addition iterated: alkene double bonds break open and chain together into poly(alkenes), the plastic family. One monomer's repeat unit echoes down a chain thousands long.
keyPoints: At AS level, addition polymerisation is the known polymerisation type.
Each monomer spends its alkene double bond, opening it to link into the growing chain.
The repeat unit mirrors the monomer minus its double bond, repeated along the chain.
Poly(alkenes) such as poly(1,2-dichloroethene) form from the corresponding substituted alkenes.

low.restatement: Every monomer donates its double bond to the chain; the polymer's backbone is single bonds with each repeat unit carrying the monomer's substituents.
low.analogy: Paperclips with a hook (double bond) that interlocks into a long strip: each clip spends its hook joining to neighbours.
low.examPointer: When drawing polymers, strip the C=C from the repeat unit and add continuing bonds through the brackets.

medium.restatement: Polymerisation conserves atoms exactly - the chain is the monomer collection linked end to end. Substituents (chlorine atoms in dichloroethene) ride along unchanged on the saturated backbone.
medium.analogy: A train built from identical carriages: each carriage (repeat unit) keeps its passengers (substituents) while couplings (single bonds) replace the open hooks (double bonds).
medium.examPointer: Check atom conservation in repeat-unit questions: nothing is lost in addition polymerisation.

check.stem: Addition polymerisation works by

options.text: Breaking open alkene double bonds to link monomers into a chain
options.explanation: The spent double bonds become the single-bond backbone of the polymer.

options.text: Splitting a polymer with water into monomers
options.explanation: That is the reverse idea, hydrolysis of polymers.
No substitution occurs; monomers simply link.
No combustion is involved.

check.stem: In the polymer from 1,2-dichloroethene, the repeat unit

options.text: Carries the two chlorine atoms on its two carbons, with the double bond consumed
options.explanation: The monomer's substituents ride into the repeat unit intact.

options.text: Loses its chlorine atoms during polymerisation
options.explanation: Addition polymerisation conserves all atoms.

options.text: Keeps its double bond inside the chain
options.explanation: The double bond is spent making the links.

options.text: Gains extra carbons from the catalyst
options.explanation: No carbons are added; the catalyst is not part of the chain.

check.stem: The polymer backbone of an addition polymer consists of

options.text: Single carbon-carbon bonds linking the repeat units
options.explanation: Spent double bonds become the saturated backbone.
The double bonds are consumed in linking.
Halogen bonds are side substituents, not backbone.
The chain is covalent throughout.

check.stem: Which statement about atom conservation in addition polymerisation is correct?

options.text: Every atom of every monomer appears in the polymer
options.explanation: Addition polymerisation loses nothing - n monomers give one chain of n repeat units.

options.text: Small molecules are eliminated as the chain grows
options.explanation: That describes condensation polymerisation, not addition.

options.text: Half the monomer mass becomes waste
options.explanation: Nothing is wasted in addition polymerisation.

options.text: Only carbon and hydrogen enter the chain
options.explanation: Substituents like chlorine enter too.

check.stem: The monomer for a poly(alkene) must contain

options.explanation: The openable double bond is the polymerisation handle.
Alkynes are not the AS-level polymerisation case.
Halogen-free alkenes like ethene polymerise readily.
Esters belong to condensation chemistry.

check.stem: State what happens to the alkene double bond during addition polymerisation.
check.modelAnswer: It breaks open, and its electrons form the single bonds joining monomers into the chain.

check.stem: Name the polymerisation type known at AS level.
Explain why addition polymerisation conserves atoms completely.
check.modelAnswer: No small molecule is eliminated: the chain is simply the monomers' atoms relinked through spent double bonds, so n monomers give a repeat-unit chain carrying every atom.

check.stem: A polymer sample is poly(1,2-dichloroethene). State the monomer and the fate of its double bond.
check.modelAnswer: The monomer is 1,2-dichloroethene; its double bond breaks open and becomes the single-bond linkage within the chain, both chlorine atoms riding on the repeat unit.

glossary.definition: A reaction joining two reactants into a single product, typically across the alkene double bond.
A reaction removing a small molecule from a larger one, leaving an alkene and the castoff fragment.
A reaction in which water splits a compound into fragments.
Chain growth where alkene monomers open their double bonds and link end to end into a saturated backbone.
